intro: My, your, his, her, its, our, their show who something belongs to. They never change with the thing you own, but “his” and “her” depend on the owner: a man → his, a woman → her.
objectifs: Know the seven possessive adjectives and match them with the subject pronouns.
Choose between his and her by the owner (a man or a woman), not by the thing.
Use a possessive with parts of the body and clothes.
Don't confuse its / it's, their / there / they're, your / you're.

texte: The possessive adjective goes before the noun. It never changes: not in the plural, not with the gender of the thing. “My car, my cars”; “their house, their houses”.
Never use an article with a possessive: “my book”, never “the my book” or “a my friend” (say “a friend of mine”, which you will see later).

sections.titre: His or her? Look at the owner
texte: In English, “his” or “her” depends on the OWNER: if the owner is a man or a boy, his; if the owner is a woman or a girl, her. The thing doesn't matter.

So: Paul and his sister (Paul's sister); Marie and her brother (Marie's brother); Marie and her husband; Paul and his wife. In languages like French, the word changes with the thing, so this is a very common mistake.

lignes: The dog is eating its food.

exemples: Sophie is talking to her son.
The company is moving its office to Lille.

texte: English almost always uses a possessive with parts of the body and the clothes a person wears: I wash my hands, She's putting on her coat, He's got his hands in his pockets. Many languages use “the” here; English doesn't.
With “have got” and descriptions, you don't need a possessive: She's got long hair. But for an action on your body, the possessive is necessary.
exemples: I brush my teeth twice a day.

sections.titre: Your, their, its: one or more owners
texte: “Your” is for one person or many people, friendly or formal: “your car” can belong to one friend, a customer, or a group.
“Their” is for several owners. Like “they”, it can also mean one person when you don't know their gender: Every student needs their own laptop.
“Its” is for a thing, an animal you don't know, a company, a country or a city: The city is famous for its museums.
exemples: Canada is famous for its lakes.

texte: Some possessives sound exactly like other words. When you speak, there is no problem; in writing, it is a common mistake, even for native speakers.
Tip: if you can say “it is”, “they are” or “you are”, you need the apostrophe (it's, they're, you're). A possessive never has an apostrophe.

lignes: The cat is eating its dinner. It's hungry.
they're (= they are), there (in that place)
They're in their car, over there.

formule: I → my · you → your · he → his · she → her · it → its · we → our · they → their (+ noun, never an article)
prononciation: “his” /hɪz/: breathed h + voiced z. Without the h, it sounds like “is”.
“her” is /hɜː/ when strong; in fast speech, often /ə/: Call her mother /ˈkɔːl ə ˈmʌðə/.
“their”, “there” and “they're” all sound like /ðeə/; “your” and “you're” like /jɔː/; “its” and “it's” like /ɪts/.
“our” /ˈaʊə/ sounds like “hour” (the h in hour is silent).
Possessives are normally weak. Stress them for contrast: It's MY bag, not YOUR bag.
erreurs: The possessive depends on the owner (Marie = her).
Use a possessive with parts of the body.
Never an article with a possessive.
The possessive of they is their.

dialogue.contexte: At a family party in Ottawa, Mia shows photos to her new colleague, Fatou.
lignes: Look, this is my family. These are my parents, and that's my brother Leo with his wife.
Yes! Her name is Chloé. She's eight months old.
She's beautiful. And who's the woman with the red hat?
That's my aunt Rose and her dog, Max. Max loves his red ball!
Ha ha! Our dog is the same. Its favourite toy is an old shoe.
And what about your family? Are your parents in Senegal?
Yes, they are. Their house is in Dakar, near the sea.

mots: a boy or man with the same parents as you
a girl or woman with the same parents as you
Paul and his wife are French.
the woman a person is married to
Anna and her husband live in Québec.
the man a person is married to
the part of your body at the end of your arm
Put on your coat. It's cold.
liked more than all the others (US: favorite)
belonging to that person, not to others

exercices.consigne: Complete with the possessive that matches the subject.

items: Mr Kamga is talking to ___ daughter.
Awa and ___ husband live in Liège.

exercices.titre: 3. Its, it's, their, they're, your, you're
items: The company is changing (its / it's) logo.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I brush the teeth every morning.
I brush my teeth every morning.
The cat is playing with it's toy.
The cat is playing with its toy.

exercices.consigne: Complete the sentence with the right possessive.
items: Pierre and ___ sister live in Lyon.

exercices.consigne: Describe a photo of your family or friends in four sentences. Use at least four different possessives (including his and her).
items: This is my brother Joël and his wife, Nadia. Her family is from Morocco. Their children are seven and ten. Our parents live with them in Brussels.

a_retenir: my, your, his, her, its, our, their + noun. They never change and never take an article.
His / her depends on the owner: Paul and his sister, Marie and her brother.
Use a possessive with the body and clothes: I wash my hands, Put on your coat.
its (possessive) ≠ it's (it is); their ≠ they're ≠ there; your ≠ you're.
Its for a thing, an animal, a company, a country.
